rows.q: Katz says there is no economy. A sceptical economist replies that markets obviously coordinate millions of decisions with no center at all. How would Katz answer, and where is his answer weakest?
rows.a:
## What "there is no economy" claims

Start with what Katz is denying, because it is easy to hear something cruder. He does not deny that people trade, set prices or coordinate without being told what to do. He denies that "the economy" is a self-standing sphere with its own laws, sitting underneath politics and ritual and explaining them. His formula in the late essays is blunt: "There is no “economy.” There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1)).

"The center" is the key term here. In Center Study it means whatever holds a community's shared attention and distributes from that position. It begins with the object everyone converges on in the originary scene and continues in whoever occupies the place of authority. Katz is saying that the economist has the order of explanation backwards: "Power is ontologically prior to and causative of, markets and all the rest" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-2)).

## How Katz would answer the economist

**1. He concedes the Hayekian point, then says it proves less than it seems to.** He does not dispute that knowledge is too distributed to be gathered at one point. He calls that argument "of course true, but also a non-sequitur and a distraction" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-12)). His analogy is a general. The general cannot know what a given platoon will face, so he leaves it leeway, and its members improvise "exchanges" of knowledge and skill among themselves. None of that makes the general's command fictional. So the market argument really says "no more than that you can’t do a very good job if you’re being micromanaged at every point along the way. It’s equally true that you can’t do a very good job if the terms of each move you make have to be “negotiated” with a constantly changing range of agents" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-25)).

**2. He redefines the market as a capillary, not a foundation.** A market is "what people without direct authority for maintaining the social center do with knowledge, information and skills when they are being protected and bounded but not directly supervised by such authorities" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-1)). The important words are *protected and bounded*. Spontaneous coordination is real, but it happens inside a space someone holds open. In his reply to the economist, the error is a reversal: "Liberalism has generated the illusion that what appears below the threshold of direct supervision is what, in fact, determines the form of supervision" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-15)). He would ask any businessman whether he could protect himself against fraud, robbery and extortion without the state, and answer for him that none believes it.

**3. He points to what the market cannot generate for itself.** Money, contract and property have to be issued and enforced. Drawing on Colin Drumm, Katz argues that a dealer can only "make a market" because someone with vastly deeper reserves stands behind him, so "something like a “lender of last resort” is constitutive of any market" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-62)). Read this way, money is a sign of the debt we owe to the center. The coordination the economist admires runs on a medium issued from a point that is not itself a market participant. In an older post he adds a moral version of the same point: the market "relies upon, and would collapse without," shared commitments it does not produce, such as "the sacrality of the individual soul" ([On Deferral](/post/on-deferral#p-8)).

**4. He denies that the center has to be a planner.** This guards against the obvious retort ("so you want Gosplan?"). The center "need not be thought of as a planning center; rather, it is the result of continual sifting, filtering, testing, mapping, simulating performed on data," and "every point of decision making is irreducible and the authority needed to make each decision is to be respected" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3)).

To see how this works, take the economist's own case: a farmer sells apples at a market price nobody set. Katz does not deny that the price emerged spontaneously. He asks what made the scene possible: a currency nobody at the stall issued, a court the buyer could go to if cheated, a dealer who will hold apples overnight because a bank will lend to him, a road someone secured. The price is spontaneous. The scene it happens on is not.

## Where the answer is weakest

**Equivocation on "coordination."** The economist's claim is epistemic: prices aggregate dispersed information that no one could gather in one place. Katz's reply is mostly about preconditions: markets need law, money and protection. Both can be true at once. Showing that a center enables the scene does not show that the center does the coordinating, and Katz has already granted the Hayekian point. A sharp economist would say: "Fine, there is a referee. The referee still doesn't play the game." Katz has his strongest material against this in the Drumm and Bichler–Nitzan line, the claim that pricing is itself shaped by power and by access to the outside spread. But that is a further argument, and it does not follow from the general thesis.

**He concedes the scale.** In one essay Katz grants that "there will be all kinds of “interfaces” where the market rules in the sense a liberal economist means. It may be that majority, even the vast majority, of transactions take place at such interfaces" ([What are We Talking About When We Talk About the Market?](/post/what-are-we-talking-about-when-we-talk-about-the-market-gablog#p-16)). His claim then shrinks to this: disciplined production by teams with clear chains of command should *set the tone* for mass exchange. That is defensible, but it is a much weaker claim than "there is no economy."

**Replacing prices.** When Katz imagines going beyond the market rather than simply re-describing it, he names the problem himself: "the notorious pricing problem, which is taken to be the doom of non-capitalistic systems," and "the only way of obtaining the needed information without prices is to close off the system, which is precisely what is deemed either impossible or terrifying" ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-16), [p-18](/post/monopoly#p-18)). He offers two substitutes:

- "controlled usurpations," where firms on a supply chain test one another by cultivating potential replacement leaders inside each other ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-21));
- succession rankings, so that "fluctuations in succession replicate price change by providing information about who will be directing a particular link in the supply chain" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)).

These are inventive. But they signal *who is reliable*, not *how scarce steel is relative to rubber this month*. Katz admits the speculative status himself: "if that’s utopian, so be it" ([Can Networks Crowd Out Markets?](/post/can-networks-crowd-out-markets-gablog#p-5)).

**A competent center is assumed.** His answer to the public-choice objection, that regulation serves whoever captures it, is that capture is a symptom of divided authority. But his alternative "presupposes a competent central authority" ([What are We Talking About…](/post/what-are-we-talking-about-when-we-talk-about-the-market-gablog#p-18)). The economist's question is precisely what happens when that competence fails, and Katz's main answer is the long-term reliance on succession.

**The history.** The origin story that "markets are created by states" leans on Graeber and Seaford. (From outside the archive: Graeber's account is contested among economic historians.) Even if it holds, an origin in state provisioning doesn't settle how mature markets work now. Katz's general view that every origin is iterated in the present gives him a reply, but he would need to make it explicitly.

## Where to read next

- [Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution) from *Anthropomorphics*. This is the fullest single statement: the Hayek concession, the thought experiment of the king who privatizes everything until monopolies form, and the "paradox of power."
- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf), with Zack Baker. It works through money, Drumm's inside and outside spreads, and derivatives as ritual. This is where his strongest reply on pricing as power lives.

As an exercise, take one price you paid this week and list every point at which some authority, rather than buyer and seller, made that exchange possible. Then ask whether any item on your list actually *determined the number*. Where you can answer yes, Katz's argument is strongest; where you can't, the economist's is.

rows.q: I run a 40-person company and two senior people are fighting over who leads a new product. Use imperative exchange, the pointman and succession to tell me what to do on Monday.
rows.a:
The short version first: **don't split the product, don't put it to a vote, and don't let it drag on. Decide it yourself on Monday, name a second as well as a first, and make both a matter of succession, not a prize.** Here is why, in Katz's terms.

## What the fight is

Two senior people want the same thing. For Center Study, that is mimetic rivalry at its most basic. Each wants the product partly *because the other wants it*. In the second lecture Katz writes that "imitation leads to rivalry because we learn to desire from our models and must therefore ultimately desire the destruction and our replacement of those models" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-8)). They have probably learned a lot from each other, and that is why it has turned into a fight.

The less comfortable part is that their fight is also aimed at you. Katz argues that when people resent each other inside an order, the resentment really goes toward the center for failing to settle things: "your resentment is, in fact, directed toward the center: the center has failed to ensure that the rules have been followed, and so you consider lifting your obligation to follow those rules yourself" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-24)).

Every day the leadership question stays open, each of them reads it as a sign that the post can be taken by whoever pushes hardest. The open question is causing the escalation.

## The pointman: one person, and that person is you

Katz's name for whoever occupies the center is the pointman. The pointman is "at the point, taking the initiative, gathering all initiatives under his banner, and at the same time the one everyone points to, out of wonder, curiosity or outrage, with the finger of accusation" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-16)).

You are the pointman of the company. Whoever leads the product will be the pointman of the product. Two things follow.

**Co-leadership is not an option.** "Only one person can occupy the center at a time, just like only one person can speak at a time in a conversation," and "leadership is successful to the extent that everyone knows their place in the order at a given point in the process" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-7)). Joint leadership only moves the fight into every meeting.

**Consensus is not an option either.** Katz says plainly that the consensus model is "so obviously a way for everyone to evade responsibility" ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-10)). Asking the team to weigh in, or hoping the two work it out, hands your decision to the rivalry.

## The criterion: who defers, and who can name a successor

Katz gives two tests you can use.

**Deferral.** For Katz, power begins in deferral: "some members of any group, in any situation, will exhibit greater powers of deferral: they will be able to stop and examine a situation while others are rushing in, and they will have the patience to wait" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-46)).

So look at how each of them has behaved during this fight. Ask yourself:
- Who kept the work moving while the question was open?
- Who has been campaigning?
- Who has been building?

The fight is itself the audition. It is evidence about each of them.

**Succession.** This is the core of Katz's political thinking, and he applies it to every institution, not only states. "If you are not choosing your successor you are not actually in power" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). The aim is to choose "the best person who will also be best in choosing a successor" ([same, ¶4](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)).

So ask each of them, separately: *if this product succeeds and you move up, who runs it after you, and how will you get them ready?* Whoever can answer concretely is thinking about the product as something that has to last. Whoever cannot is thinking about a title.

## Monday, as an imperative exchange

The imperative exchange is the basic relation to the center. A command comes from the center, and a request goes back that amounts to "tell me how to serve you" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-40)). In its mature form the request is "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)).

Your job on Monday is to issue a command clear enough that both of them can answer it in that form. Here is the sequence, which is my application of Katz to your situation:

1. **Meet each of them separately first.** Tell each your decision before anyone else hears it. Hear the objection once. Do not reopen the question.

2. **Issue the command with power and responsibility matched.** "Power should always be matched with responsibility" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-61)). The new lead gets the budget, the hiring and the deadlines, and is answerable for the result. Spell out all of it, because whatever you leave vague becomes the next fight.

3. **Name the other person second, publicly, and give them a real assignment.** Katz's model is that "each institution has a head, and this head has an appointed successor... But the appointed successor will be assessed and replaced regularly" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)). Being named second is not a consolation prize. It is a standing place in the order, and it is revisable in both directions. That gives the loser something to work toward and the winner something to protect.

   If the second person can take on a parallel problem that answers directly to you, all the better. Katz calls this a skunkworks: a team "directly accountable to the central authority" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-12)). It turns their energy into competing on results.

4. **Announce it to the whole company, briefly and in person.** For Katz, succession is a public event, not a private deal. People need to know where they stand, and the two rivals need to hear it said in front of everyone.

5. **Treat what happens next as information.** Katz notes that every act of obedience means "I'm following your command, but in this way" ([The Problem of Obedience, Revisited](/post/the-problem-of-obedience-revisited#p-10)). Watch how each of them obeys over the next month. That is your evidence for any later revision.

The point of all this is not to make them stop competing. The pointman's task is to "convert these resentments into new forms of cooperation, emulation and friendly competition" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-49)). Rivalry with a settled order is useful. Rivalry with no order destroys the team.

## A caution

Katz writes mostly about states, courts and money. The concepts carry over to a 40-person company, and he says explicitly that succession applies to every institution. But the step-by-step plan above is my application of his ideas, not something he wrote about company management.

## What to read next

- [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity) is short. It explains why naming a successor is the real test of holding a post, and why the choice can be revised.
- [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf), ¶¶46–63, gives the full account of power as deferral and of how a leader handles resentment aimed at the center.

A question to take into Monday: if you had to name *your own* successor today, which of the two would it be? If the answer is different from who you will put on this product, think about why.

rows.q: What exactly is idiomclining, how is it different from coining jargon, and can you idiomcline this sentence of mine: "Our team needs better communication"?
rows.a:
## What idiomclining is

The word combines "idiom" with "cline." A cline, in linguistics, is the slow, almost invisible slide of a word from full meaning toward grammatical function. "Going to" is a standard example from outside the archive: it once described walking somewhere and is now a marker of the future tense. Katz takes the word from his earlier work on "upclining," which meant reversing that slide. The idea was "retrieving grammaticized signs and re-semanticizing them," on the hunch that a word worn smooth by use still holds a buried "memory" that can be brought back ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16)). An "upcline" resists both the passive "incline" and the catastrophic "decline" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16)).

In the older essay he describes the move as one in which "a word is deliberately removed from a circulation that splinters its uses, and placed within a new circulation, or idiom, that treats the word as a prompt for a new hierarchy of declaratives, imperatives and ostensives" ([Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-49)). His example there is "take." Before the word split into specialized cousins like "grasp" and "seize," it covered a far wider ground. Stepping back up to that wider sense is what opens new uses such as "taking responsibility."

Idiomclining generalizes this into a working habit: "setting relatively immobilized 'pieces' of language back into motion" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17)). Katz is candid that you will always be somewhat wrong when you do it, because you are breaking a convention. You also can't really fail, because your move hands others a chance to make an adjusted response. He offers it explicitly as a replacement for "critical thinking." His reason is Goodhart's law: "every single word, expression or sentence is or contains measures that are liable to become targets" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-1)). An idiom is the safeguard, because it reminds everyone that every measure is just a way of naming, one that depends on people able to look at something together and say "this is the same."

## How it differs from coining jargon

Katz does not condemn specialized vocabulary as such. He notes that "what seems like unintelligible jargon is very often a way of phrasing some claim that has resulted from the cumulative responses to attacks on a dozen previous ways of phrasing it" ([The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-4)). Compressed terms can record real work.

The difference is in the direction of motion:

- **Jargon freezes.** A coined term starts acting like a metalanguage, as though it stood outside the scene and could judge it. It becomes a badge of belonging, or something to hit as a target. Katz warns that an idiom too can "become so formulaic as to mark belonging to a impenetrable bureaucratic space," and he answers: "There must always be space for idiom generation within the idiom" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-10)).
- **Idiomclining thaws.** It breaks up stuck terms. Breaking up jargon "is the scientific equivalent of de-mythification—it’s a question of refusing the imperatives the nominalizations start giving you, the imperative exchanges they lure you into" ([Technology and Magic, Doings and Happenings](/post/technology-and-magic-doings-and-happenings#p-21)). The lure he means is the belief that a new term will itself fix the problem.
- **Idiomclining also travels.** You want your idiom "both more idiomatic and more transferable." It should be specific to this exchange and this scene, and still usable by your listener with anyone else ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-15)).

A practical warning follows. If I simply swapped "communication" in your sentence for a Center Study term like "joint attention," that would be coining jargon, not idiomclining. The result would sound deep and still give your team nothing to do.

## Idiomclining "Our team needs better communication"

Your sentence happens to contain one of the words Katz names directly. He describes his "hostility to words like 'cognition,' 'consciousness,' 'belief,' 'communication,'" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-1)). Here is how I would work on it.

**1. Name what kind of word "communication" is.** It belongs to what Katz, following the literacy scholar David Olson, calls the metalanguage of literacy: words that grade language and behavior from outside. It works like "clear" does for student writing. Such words "allow us to assess a piece of writing, but they tell us nothing about how the writing was produced" ([The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-13)). "Better communication" judges your team without telling anyone what to do. Katz has a word for that: "assessments of the language use of others devoid of operable imperatives is the way I would define 'cant'" ([On the Culling of Cant](/post/on-the-culling-of-cant#p-2)). It also invites Goodhart's law. Once you measure "communication" by meetings held or messages sent, you get more meetings and more messages.

**2. Find the imperative hidden inside the declarative.** "Needs" makes a demand, but grammatically it is addressed to no one. In Katz's grammar a demand is really a request for a command. "Whatever your demand of the center, consider the kind of command that could limit and satisfy it better than it would itself know how to and then realize that your demand is really for such a command" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-17)). So ask who would issue the command and what it would be. Teams have captains ([Hostages, Proxies, and Moles](/post/hostages-proxies-and-moles#p-5)). Your sentence leaves the captain out.

**3. Step the word back up its cline.** (The etymology here comes from outside the archive.) "Communicate" comes from the Latin *communicare*, "to make common, to share." Its older sense is not "send messages" but "bring something into the shared space." In Center Study's terms, that means putting something at the center where everyone can point to it. This recovered sense is the upcline.

**4. Rewrite in that recovered sense, tied to a scene.** Here are a few drafts, each a deliberate small mistake that invites correction:

- "What one of us sees, the one who has to act on it doesn't see in time." This moves the problem from talk to a missing shared ostensive, something everyone can point to.
- "Each of us is carrying out a different version of the same instruction." This names what Katz calls the gap between a command as issued and as obeyed. He treats that gap as the proper object of inquiry ([The Center and Imperative Authority](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-imperative-authority#p-4)).
- "We don't know who decides when we disagree." This puts back the center, meaning whoever holds authority, which the original sentence hid.

Each version can be checked: you could point to a moment when it held. Each also suggests its own next step. The first asks for a common point of reference. The second asks for the instruction to be made more explicit. The third asks for clear lines of authority. They are not interchangeable, so choosing among them is a real diagnosis of your team.

Try this: describe one recent moment when things went wrong on your team, and say which of the three versions fits it, or what fits better. Your account of that moment will be more idiomatic than any of my drafts.

## Reading next

- [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining). The essay itself is short and lays out the whole move, including Goodhart's law, why each new sign is both mistaken and productive, and the link to computation.
- [Technology and Magic, Doings and Happenings](/post/technology-and-magic-doings-and-happenings). It shows how nouns made from verbs harden into jargon, and how to turn them back into verbs by asking what was done and what merely happened. That is the second half of the skill you just practiced.

rows.q: Explain how the ostensive, imperative and declarative relate to Katz's account of money as debt to the center, for someone who knows Girard well but has never read Gans.
rows.a:
## Starting from Girard: the sign rather than the murder

You already have most of what you need. Gans, and Katz after him, keep Girard's mimetic anthropology: desire learned from a model, rivalry, a crisis that threatens the group. What changes is how the crisis resolves. Katz puts the objection to Girard bluntly: "there’s no reason why some animal group, even an exceptionally intelligent one, should view ganging up on and killing one of its members as “meaningful,” which is to say, “memorable.”" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-38)).

Something has to make the event memorable and repeatable, and that something is a sign. Once you add it, Gans realised, "if the real point is the pointing, the killing itself is superfluous" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-39)). So in Gans's originary scene the group converges on an object, usually food. One member hesitates, and his grasping movement becomes a gesture of aborted appropriation. The others imitate the gesture rather than the grab. Katz calls this "Gans’s transcendence of Girard": "the kind of “counter-imitation” involved in the sign arrests rather than accelerating mimetic rivalry" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-12)).

The point that matters for money is this: in Gans's scene the object at the center is not a victim but a giver. It holds the group back and then lets itself be shared. Katz draws the consequence directly. The exchange with the center is "an asymmetrical exchange, with the center first giving and those on the periphery then responding in kind, makes talk of debt unavoidable" ([Data as Currency and the Debt to the Center](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-1)). That is why he can write: "we’re all indebted to the center—this is originary, not modern" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)). Money is not where debt begins. Money is one late form of a debt as old as language.

The three speech forms can be read as three stages in how that debt is carried.

## The ostensive: acknowledging the giver

The first sign is ostensive, a pointing. It names the central object and in doing so defers appropriating it. In debt terms, the ostensive is the bare acknowledgement that what we are about to share comes from the center. Each participant receives a portion only because everyone has first shown, through the sign, that they are not seizing it.

This is also where Gans parts from Girard on the historical record, and Katz finds it important. The earliest communities sacrificed to animal deities, and human sacrifice comes "at a much later, imperial state" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3)). On Katz's account, human sacrifice is not the origin. It is what an inflated debt eventually demands.

## The imperative: debt becomes an exchange

The imperative arises from a mistake. An "inappropriate ostensive": "One member of the community issues the ostensive sign in the absence of the object, and another member of the community then supplies the object" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-1)). Naming something absent becomes a demand that it be brought.

Applied to the center, this gives Katz's key concept for ritual, *imperative exchange*: "we pray to God and God issues commands to us... if we do what God says we can expect our requests to Him to be honored" ([Felicity](/post/felicity#p-11)). Sacrifice is exactly this. The worshipper obeys an order to return part of what the deity provided and, in the same act, asks for more ([Beyond “Post-Sacrificial”](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-1)). Debt now has terms: something is owed, there is a schedule, and a counter-request is attached.

This is where your Girard enters through a different door. As the center becomes a human king and then a divine emperor, "the interval between debt issuance and dischargement grows, the debt become overwhelming, even unbearable, to the point where even the sacrifice of the first-born to the God-emperor is not enough" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3)). The sacrificial crisis Girard places at the origin, Katz places downstream, as a crisis of imperative exchange under empire. Katz's essay with Zack Baker reads the Axial Age answer the same way: in place of the emperor-god comes a God to whom "nothing less than complete donation of one’s being is acceptable" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-15)).

## The declarative: speaking on credit

The declarative arises when an imperative cannot be fulfilled because the object simply isn't there. In Gans's account the speaker repeats the object's name together with an interdiction, a "don't." Katz adds an amendment that is central to the money question. The "don't" points two ways. It tells the one making the demand to stop, and it tells the object itself to stay away, which only the center could command. So "the imperator is told to cease and desist “because” the object has been ordered away" ([Felicity](/post/felicity#p-19); see also [Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-7)). The declarative is how "reality" first appears: an order of things that answers to the center and not to my demands.

Katz then puts this in the language of finance. The declarative "involves a kind of “loan” or “credit” from the center, which must be backing a scene", and so "to speak in sentences is to draw upon and issue lines of credit" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-8)). A sentence asks you to accept, for now, a state of things you cannot check on the spot, and to wait. Elsewhere Katz says the same of promises: "A promise draws credit from the promisee and places one in debt" ([Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-10)). He extends it to all speech: "every utterance is to some extent a promise, at least regarding the ostensive conditions under which its truth will be affirmed" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-12)).

## Money: the declarative's structure, issued by an occupied center

Now money. After the "Big Man" seizes the ritual center and takes over distribution, the center is occupied by a person and no longer a single scene everyone attends. Money is how that occupied center keeps the debt in circulation across the gaps. Gans's own definition, which Katz takes up, is that money is "a credit drawn on the sacred that cannot be freely reproduced" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-10)). Katz and Baker go further: "money is the means through which the imperial center extends the indebtedness of its subjects by spreading this indebtedness differentially and asymmetrically among its subjects" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-29)).

Put the three forms together and you get the shape of the argument. The essay itself doesn't state it in these words; this is my reading of how the pieces fit. Money stands to the imperative exchange of ritual as the declarative stands to the imperative. It lets a debt to the center be acknowledged and discharged "later and elsewhere" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-18)), outside the presence of the ritual scene, by holding a virtual present open. The everyday cash sale that seems to settle a debt instantly depends on that held-open present: "Instantaneity or simultaneity is a fiction, or virtual, and the interval within which an exchange can be considered instantaneous depends upon the extent to which the relation between the indebted subject and the debt imposing and money issuing institutions remains the same over time" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-31)).

That is why Katz ties money so closely to succession. A note, like a sentence, is good only if the center that backs it can be expected to still be the same center when the note is redeemed.

## Where this goes in Katz's own project

Katz does not stop at description. If speech is already credit, then money can in principle give way to what he calls data exchange and "learncoin": accreditation tied to pedagogy and succession instead of discounting against expected earnings. He states the starting point plainly in [Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection: Expectant Scenes](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes#p-6): "An imperative, whether it be a command, demand or anything in between, always looks forward to some exchange." That later programme is contested even among sympathetic readers. Treat it as Katz's wager, not as a consequence the grammar forces.

## What to read next

- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf) (with Zack Baker). The fullest treatment, from the Big Man through the Bank of England to derivatives as ritual. Start here.
- [Felicity](/post/felicity), then [Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality). These give the grammar step by step, ending with the declarative as a "line of credit."
- For the Gans–Girard divergence in more detail, read [Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-38) from the cited paragraph onward.

An exercise that uses your Girard: take a scapegoating episode you know well, for instance from Girard's *The Scapegoat*. Ask what debt the community believed it owed, to what center, and what had gone wrong in the imperative exchange that made a human life seem the only adequate payment. Then compare your answer with Katz's claim that human sacrifice is a symptom of an overextended debt rather than the origin of the sacred.

rows.q: Trace how the concept of the center changes from Anthropomorphics to the recent essays on thirdness and data exchange. What stayed, and what was dropped?
rows.a:
The short version: the center is the one concept that never moves. Its **primacy** stays fixed; what changes is its **medium**. In *Anthropomorphics* the center is mainly a matter of imperatives, sacrality and sovereignty. By the Thirdness and data-exchange essays it is a matter of debt, adjudication and data. And a problem Katz treated as open in 2019, the split between the "signifying" and the "occupied" center, is no longer treated as a standing problem. It gets absorbed into succession.

## The starting point: the center in *Anthropomorphics* (2019)

Three ideas organize the book.

**The center comes before the human.** Agency is attributed to the central being before it is attributed to anyone on the margin. That is where the name comes from: "The human is modeled on the non-human center… Humans anthropomorphized themselves before they could carry out this operation on anything else" ([The Center and the Declarative](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative#p-25)).

**The center has a fracture.** Once sacral kingship falls, the center splits in two. There is the *signifying* center: the sacred, or what our signs ultimately answer to. There is the *occupied* center: whoever actually rules. The book frames its central political problem as the gap between them: "There is, in any community, a central authority, the final source of imperatives; and yet those imperatives are only worthy of being followed if the central authority is in accord with the signifying center" ([The Center and Imperative Authority](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-imperative-authority#p-1)).

The rest of the book's apparatus is built around this gap:
- the **imperative gap**, the distance between a command as issued and the command as obeyed;
- **super-sovereignty**, meaning disciplines and "rights" claiming to stand above the ruler;
- the ethical stance of **"donating your resentment to the center"** ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-15)).

**Succession is the practical answer.** "The solution I propose: the current occupant of the center chooses his successor" ([Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-2)). The posture recommended to the reader is a patient infiltration, which Katz calls "a kind of inverted messianism" ([same, p-14](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-14)). You wait for the ruler who will name a successor, and you shape institutions so they are ready when that happens.

## What stayed

**The primacy of the center.** Nothing in the later essays retreats from it. "So, we’re all indebted to the center—this is originary, not modern" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)).

**Succession.** It does more than survive; it becomes the backbone of the later work. "Singularized succession in perpetuity" turns the 2019 proposal into a chain: you choose someone who will choose someone who will choose someone.

**The imperative.** Imperative exchange, with prayer as its model, carries through unchanged in substance. What changes is the phrasing: "the imperative *of* the center", and the worry about its "parceling out".

**Donating resentment to the center.** This survives as an idiom and gets a new economic sense; it is "tokenized." One later line defines the center against resentment itself: "The center doesn’t resent—that would serve as a definition of the center" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-15)).

**The seed of the later work.** It was already present in 2019: "The center is the coordination I’m seeking within the circuits of capital, technology and media" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-18)). The data-exchange period grows out of that sentence.

## What changed

### 1. The signifying/occupied split is folded into succession

This is the biggest conceptual move, and Katz names it himself, referring back to the book: "Succession has served as the center of thinking about sovereignty, uniting what *Anthropomorphics* calls the “signifying center” (the sacred) and the occupied center (the imperial) in the temporality of singularized succession in perpetuity" ([Hyperstitching…](/post/hyperstitching-the-soliciting-of-the-center-and-the-prolonging-of-the-imperative#p-1)).

In 2019 the two centers had to be brought into *accord* at a given moment. Later, their unity lies in *continuity over time*, an unbroken chain of hand-offs.

The split is also redescribed. It is no longer sacred versus ruler. It becomes two features of the originary object itself: "both the thing we attend to and the meta-person we obey… It is these two “features” of the “center” that get separated" over time ([The Sample as Our Donation to the Center](/post/the-sample-as-our-donation-to-the-center#p-6)). In [Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-3) this becomes "the problem of the two centers." Imperial systems draw our attention away from the social center and towards *samples*, and we serve the center by curating those samples as data.

### 2. The center becomes central intelligence

The center increasingly reads as an informational process rather than a person or an altar. "The center need not be thought of as a planning center; rather, it is the result of continual sifting, filtering, testing, mapping, simulating performed on data… the center is whatever will turn out to have been furthest upstream of that" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3), [p-5](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-5)).

Elsewhere: "The center is now the entire data infrastructure and its algorithmic treatments that one must donate to and extract from: the central intelligence" ([Centrifugal Signifying](/post/centrifugal-signifying#p-21)).

The old imperative exchange becomes *data exchange*: "Data exchange is always with the center" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-13)).

### 3. The juridical moves to the middle

In *Anthropomorphics* justice systems belong mainly to the historical story about divine kingship and the crisis of the Axial Age. In the Thirdness essays the juridical sits between the ritual and the disciplinary. It becomes the form in which the center is actually encountered: "we place the juridical at the center—the juridical is the form taken for the settling of resentments" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-7)).

Thirdness then proposes to "transition the juridical… into data exchange." Parties to a dispute would donate data to, or receive data from, the center "in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)).

### 4. Debt replaces gift

The 2019 language of gift, sacrifice and imperative exchange becomes the language of debt, credit, enforcement and forgiveness. The modern state is redescribed as "a debt enforcement and forgiveness agency" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-1)). Money is then "a credit drawn on the sacred," following Gans, in the jointly written [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-8).

### 5. Posture: from waiting to building

The inverted messianism of 2019 becomes something more active. "There’s nothing more important, and really nothing else than, imagining and building such companies" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-15)), meaning companies that discount their value against futures beyond anyone now living.

## What was dropped, or quietly receded

Katz rarely announces that he has dropped something, so some of this is my reading of where the weight shifts.

- **Renamings he does announce.** "Occupant of the center" becomes "pointman" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)), then "dictator" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-1)), and then he wavers back towards "sovereign." "Anthropomorphics" gave way to "center study" for some years before being reclaimed ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)).
- **The rigid succession machinery of 2019.** In the book, top-tier candidates are barred from real power. Later it softens towards constant revision of rankings, which work like prices, and "controlled usurpations" between institutions. In one essay it softens even to the thought that "anyone might give ruling a try for a bit" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-12)).
- **The sacral history as the main frame.** It is not repudiated; the Axial Age returns in [The Pointman](/post/the-pointman). But it no longer carries the argument. The most recent essays state outright: "Center Study has no political theology, because what would be political theology is retracted into anthropology and anthropology is retracted into anthropomorphics" ([Deferral and Appropriation](/post/deferral-and-appropriation-property-and-the-center#p-1)).
- **"The market"** as the zone of delegation below sovereign supervision. It gives way to subscription networks of teams, and money is to give way to "learncoin."

## A question to carry forward

Test the main shift on a case. Take a dispute you know: a contested firing, say, or a defamation suit. Describe it twice. First, the 2019 way: the gap between what the occupied center commanded and what the signifying center would sanction. Then the Thirdness way: what data each party should donate to the center, and how the settlement would extend a line of succession. Which description shows you more?

## Where to read next

- **[Hyperstitching the Soliciting of the Center…](/post/hyperstitching-the-soliciting-of-the-center-and-the-prolonging-of-the-imperative)** is Katz's own compressed retrospective. It explicitly maps the old vocabulary (succession, signifying center) onto the new one (soliciting the center, perfecting the imperative).
- **[The Holding and the Held Center: Beyond Disagreement](/post/the-holding-and-the-held-center-beyond-disagreement)** is where the 2019 signifying/occupied split is reworked most directly, before it is absorbed into succession.

rows.q: Is singularized succession in perpetuity just monarchism? Give the strongest version of that objection and then Katz's reply.
rows.a:
## Short answer

No, but the objection is stronger than a quick "no" suggests, and Katz grants more of it than you might expect. He builds singularized succession in perpetuity (SSIP) out of monarchy and absolutism. What he claims to keep is the *form* of monarchy: a single occupant of the center who picks who comes next. What he claims to drop is monarchy's *content*: blood, sacral kingship, coronation, and fixed rules of inheritance. So the real question is whether keeping the form and dropping the content gives you something new, or only monarchy with the reasons for monarchy removed.

## The objection at its strongest

The objection should not stop at "this looks like monarchy." Katz admits the resemblance freely. He says the concept "was a continuation of the absolutist thinking through which I transitioned out of liberalism back in 2015-6" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)), and calls it "the successor concept to 'absolutism'" ([Selving](/post/selving#p-21)). His test for whether someone actually holds power is a monarch's test: if you do not choose your successor, whoever does choose holds the real power.

The sharper charge is this. Historical monarchy could defend itself by appeal to things beyond itself: divine sanction, natural law, the king's duty to the common good, a sacred order the king answered to. Katz removes all of that. He writes that "there is nothing more to governance than singularized succession in perpetuity," and that consent, natural right, natural law and the common good "are either dispensed with or subsumed within it" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-1)). Appeals to the common good become "apotropaic—things for a ruler to say so as to ward off incitements to rebellion" ([p-2](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-2)). He also says that SSIP "completely invalidates the 'rule of law'" ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)).

On this reading SSIP is worse than monarchism. It is absolutism with nothing left above it to judge it. It is power whose only stated purpose is to keep itself going, presented in the vocabulary of "data security" and "pedagogy." The word "perpetuity" makes things worse, because it commits the order in advance to its own continuation regardless of who holds the center. The classic objection to monarchy, the bad king, then has nowhere to go.

## Katz's reply

His answer has several parts that work together.

**1. Monarchy is a placeholder, and the concept is meant to go beyond it.** In [Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-1) he agrees with the first premise: "It is true that monarchy is the only real form of governance—everything else is either mimicking monarchy or predicated on the endless struggle to prevent others from installing 'their' king." Then he turns: "we need the concept of 'singular succession' to include all that we want in monarchy without restricting ourselves to forms of governance 'similar' to known forms of monarchy." His example is a security and technology firm that slowly absorbs the functions of a failing state, and he says there would be "no reason to assume" this process ends in the office of monarch. "Monarchy remains a placeholder concept, still indispensable in arguing with 'democrats' and 'republicans'" ([p-4](/post/continuum-of-power#p-4)). The range of possibilities runs from primogeniture to "rapid transfers of power from one figure to another," which he compares to a manager bringing in relief pitchers one after another. In that version, "Occupation of the center would be completely desacralized and de-divinized... and reduced to functionality" ([p-5](/post/continuum-of-power#p-5)). He even says the "multiplication of succession rituals would distinguish this order from monarchy, which has few and regularly set succession rituals (coronations)" ([p-3](/post/continuum-of-power#p-3)).

**2. It works against the dynastic principle.** SSIP "cuts against, without excluding... primogeniture, since succession is now understood as the outcome of competition and mentorship" ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)). Hereditary rule settles the succession problem "but in such a way as to generate other problems," such as the king who dies without an heir ([The Sufficiency of SSIP](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)). The successor's position is also never fixed for good: "The selection would not be made once and for all, in the form of a permanent vice-president" ([p-8](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-8)). The choice is revised as conditions and candidates change. In [Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-12) he says that once losing the throne no longer means death, his scheme starts to approach sortition, the choosing of rulers by lot.

**3. It describes how any practice survives, not only how states are governed.** This is the move that most separates it from monarchism. "I want the concept to be descriptive in a revealing way rather than simply normative... succession posits the assumption that this is what we're always doing" ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)). Any practice, not only rule, can be judged this way: "you could define a practice in terms of the singularization of the one who will succeed it" ([Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics#p-27)). The concept also reaches down to ordinary people, each of whom is to exercise it "in the way appropriate to whatever disciplinary spaces each and every one of us is implicated in" ([Language, the Ultimate Source and Analysis of Data](/post/language-the-ultimate-source-and-analysis-of-data#p-7)). A teacher training a replacement, a founder building a company meant to outlast him, a scholar trying to leave a line of inquiry behind: in Katz's vocabulary each of these is succession, and monarchy is simply the place where it is most visible.

**4. "Perpetuity" is the part that does the critical work.** The concept is not "the king names whoever he likes." It asks for "the best person who will also be best in choosing a successor, seeing to all the conditions enabling that successor, who will best choose his successor, and so on" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). Holding that long horizon is how the concept tells genuine rule apart from mere strongman rule: "It's interesting that the 'totalitarian' leaders never publicly—and, probably, privately, for that matter—choose a successor" ([p-9](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-9)). Seen this way, a dictator who refuses to plan his succession fails the test, and most historical despots would fail it. The long horizon also gives SSIP its other opponent, capital's habit of "discounting against expected future earnings," whose time frame always stops short of real continuity ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-6)).

**5. It does not dictate a regime's content.** Katz admits the formula is "'formal,' and not... as rich in content as proposed modes of government based on some kind of 'substantial' identity, like creed, nation, or race. But not only does it not exclude any particular basis for social order, it provides a powerful principle of selection of one over another" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-10)). Elsewhere he says the originary hypothesis is "not intrinsically committed or opposed to monarchy or democracy, fascism or communism" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-6)). The concept is meant to test whatever program you hold: how would your Christian nationalism, or your Prometheanism, increase the likelihood of a center that can see to its own succession? ([Staged Succession](/post/staged-succession-marginalizing-the-victimary-and-scapegoating-in-a-single-move#p-15)).

**6. On the bad king.** Katz's first answer is that a bad ruler cannot actually name a successor who will take hold. Doing so would upset the factions he depends on: "If the president of the US were actually the chief executive and commander-in-chief it wouldn't be Joe Biden" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-7)). Naming a successor demands real command, so the test screens rulers out as well as in. His second answer is legal. The ruler can be sued, but with high stakes on both sides: "If the president could seek to remove from power and impose further penalties on those participating in a failed impeachment and removal attempt, impeachment would become an entirely different proposition" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-17)). Removing a ruler stays possible, but it costs the challenger something and is no longer a routine move in party politics.

## Where the objection still has force

Katz's reply shows that SSIP is not *traditional* monarchism. It is not nostalgic, it is not hereditary, it is not sacral, and it is not committed to any particular regime. It does not show that the concept escapes the charge of power justifying itself. His answer to that charge is the anthropology underneath: the continuity of the center is "the umbilical cord linking us to the originary scene" ([Nomos](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-2)), the first thing the center demands, prior to any idea of the good. If you accept the originary hypothesis, sustaining the center is not empty, because it is the condition for anything else being good. If you do not accept it, the objection stands. Note too that several of his safeguards (trust among elites, reliable data, judges loyal to the system) are presented in Rotating Dictatorship as things he assumes rather than things the concept guarantees.

## What to read next

- [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity) is Katz's most direct defense of the concept, and it takes up the bad-ruler objection by name.
- [Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power) is where he separates SSIP from monarchy explicitly and links it to his critique of bureaucracy.

**An exercise:** pick an institution you know well, such as a department, a company or a church. Ask who actually chooses the next head, and what that choice tells you about where power in it really sits. Then ask whether the answer matches the official account. By Katz's test, that gap is where the institution's real politics happens.

rows.q: On Katz's account, why can a language model write fluent declaratives but not promise or deem? Does that argument hold up?
rows.a:
## The short answer

On Katz's account, a promise or an act of deeming is not a kind of sentence. It is a move on a scene that puts the speaker in debt to the center and leaves him exposed to whoever can hold him to it. A language model can produce the form. It cannot stand where the speaker of a promise has to stand. The declarative seems different because literacy, and the metaphysics built on it, taught us to read declaratives as if they needed no speaker at all.

So the asymmetry in your question is real, but on Katz's own terms it is shallower than it looks. I'll take the two halves in turn and then weigh the argument.

## Why the declarative comes easily

For Katz, following Gans, the declarative is the latest and most detachable of the speech forms. It grows out of a failed imperative and lets us refer to what is absent. Writing then made it "isolatable and analyzable as a speech form" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-2)). The metalanguage of literacy turned it into the model of language as such, aiming at a sentence "that could be uttered felicitously by anyone, anywhere, at any time" ([An Introduction to Disciplinarity](/post/introduction-to-disciplinarity#p-87)).

A language model is that "anyone." It is trained on the archive of the declarative order: text already stripped of the scenes that produced it. In Katz's idiom, it is metaphysics realised in a machine. It is fluent in exactly the form our culture had already learned to treat as self-standing.

## Why promising and deeming are different

The main passage is in [Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-12). An AI can be trained to name things, "but AIs can't “deem,” or if they do deem, they have been authorized or deemed worthy to do so, by, ultimately, a human." Deeming "places us in the chain of originary debt to the center." It belongs to a cluster of ostensive-imperative acts: promise, prayer, oath, curse, bless, oblige, thank. These are "uncannily similar to programming" ([p-13](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-13)), which is why the question presses on us now.

Three lines of his thought converge here.

1. **A promise is a debt.** "A promise draws credit from the promisee and places one in debt" ([Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-10)). Debt means someone can enforce it or forgive it. A model has nothing that can be called in, so the credit has nowhere to land.

2. **Reliability comes before predictability.** Katz insists that "promising, indebting, and issuing credit are speech acts that cannot be reduced to computation, and are therefore the domain of decision." A promise does contain predictions, but "broader conditions of predictability are necessary for these more localized predictions to be possible and those broader conditions require humans to be reliable before they are predictable" ([p-12](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-12)). A model is all prediction. The reliability that prediction rests on has to be supplied by someone else.

3. **The sign begins as exposure.** On the originary scene the gesture means something only because "each participant exposes himself to the possible violence of others" ([A Kind of Apocalyptic Politics](/post/a-kind-of-apocalyptic-politics#p-3)). A promise repeats that exposure in a civilised form. Hence Katz's line: "We can't credit a machine's promise, even if we fully expect it to do what it says it will" ([Curriculum, p-14](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-14)). Programming a promise would only reveal "that we weren't really doing it precisely because being programmed negates those speech acts" ([p-17](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-17)).

## Does it hold up?

Partly, and Katz's own framework gives you the tools to see where it bends.

**Where it holds.** The structural argument is strong. If performatives get their force from standing and liability rather than from their form, then a speaker that cannot be held to anything cannot promise. That claim does not depend on what goes on "inside" the machine. It is a claim about the scene: who answers, to whom, and through which chain back to the center. It also makes sense of a practical intuition: when a company's chatbot "promises" a refund, we look for the company. The debt flows up to whoever deployed it.

**Where it is weaker.**

- **Katz calls it a hypothesis.** His claim that a machine's simulated promise will always feel "off" in a way humans can detect is offered "as a hypothesis that I as yet have no idea how to prove or disprove" ([p-14](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-14)). He is also wary of that kind of test elsewhere: "lists of things humans can do that machines can't merely provide a menu of AI improvements for the next generation of programmers to attempt" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-10)). The detectable "off-ness" is the vulnerable part of the argument. The structural point about debt is the durable part, and Katz himself says the Turing-style question matters only as a model for "performing our relations to the scenes we are on" ([p-15](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-15)).

- **Delegation is already built in.** He leaves open that an AI could deem if it has been "authorized … by, ultimately, a human." That means the real claim is narrower than "machines can't promise." It is that machines can't originate a promise: they can relay one whose debt sits with a human or a team. That fits his centered ordinality, where nearly every human speaker also relays authority from further up. So the human/machine line becomes a matter of where the chain of liability ends, not a difference in kind at each link.

- **Declaratives are promises too.** This is the turn I think matters most. Katz says "every utterance is to some extent a promise, at least regarding the ostensive conditions under which its truth will be affirmed" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-12)). Any declarative leaves its speaker "implicitly … open to ostensive verification" ([Political Syntax (III)](/post/political-syntax-iii-and-originary-thinking#p-6)). If that is right, the model's fluent declaratives are also unbacked. They only look complete because literacy trained us to read the declarative as scene-free. The real line is not between declaratives (which machines manage) and performatives (which they don't). It runs through every utterance: no one stands behind the model's output except whoever chooses to put their credit on it.

My overall judgment is that the argument holds as an account of where liability sits. It is shakier as a prediction about what people will be able to detect. The shakiness matters less than it seems, because Katz's project is not to rescue a human essence. It is to make our own promising, deeming and ledgering more explicit, since "We are all “marked up” indelibly in ways no algorithm or program ever can be" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-26)).

## Where to read next

- [Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah): the fullest account of the promise as debt and credit, and of blockchains as ways of locking promises in. Recording a promise is ledgering, not promising, and that distinction sharpens your question.
- [Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human): Katz's other attempt at a human/machine boundary (humans "tag in order to track"). It is worth comparing with the deeming argument.

**An exercise:** take a sentence an AI produced for you that you found useful. Ask what you would have to do to make it a promise: who would have to stand behind it, and with what at risk. That answer shows you, in Katz's terms, where the center actually is in your exchange with the machine.

rows.q: Take the essays on Judaism as a civilizational blockchain. What is the argument, and how does it follow from the originary hypothesis?
rows.a:
## The argument in brief

"Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain" proposes a vocation for Jews. Katz does not want it to be a defence against antisemitism or a claim to victimhood. He wants a role that follows from how hostility to Jews works. The essay moves in four steps.

**1. The structure of the hostility.** Katz prefers "the Jews as scandal" to "antisemitism." The scandal is that Jewish existence gets read as proof of hidden, monstrous power. The consequence is that the enemy of the Jews concludes the system itself is captured: "Erasing the scandal of the Jews requires operating extra-juridically, even extra-systemically, precisely because the Jews control all that and make it impossible to obtain 'justice,' with the proof of that being, tautologically, their existence" ([Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-2)). He calls this "collective fantasy" because it defeats itself: "If the Jews really control everything, there's nothing you can do; if you can do something, they don't really control everything" ([p-3](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-3)). Once you admit some Jewish power, it becomes one measurable power among others, and the grievance has to go through ordinary channels.

**2. The vocation that hostility implies.** Since the war on the Jews takes the form of a vendetta that has to bypass judgment, the opposite role suggests itself: "that the war against the Jews implies a comprehensive vendetta does suggest a kind of vocation for the Jews themselves: maintaining all the institutional means of deferring vendetta" ([p-6](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-6)). Jews will not be left alone in any case. They "have no choice but to represent something" ([p-8](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-8)), so they may as well represent something they choose.

**3. Witnessing, narrowed down.** The old idea that Jews bear witness to injustice is kept but restricted. It stops being a mandate for "social justice" and is limited "strictly to the operation of the juridical within the terms of the nomos" ([p-9](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-9)). That means actual cases, between actual parties, under rules of evidence. From this comes the central image: Jews as a civilizational blockchain, "recording social exchanges and disputes as objectively and permanently as we can" ([p-11](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-11)). Katz condenses it into a stance toward the nations: "we will mark your treatment of us on the scale of justice while marking as deviant anyone claiming adherence to Judaism who seeks to undermine covenants, or contracts or agreements" ([p-14](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-14)).

**4. What gets recorded.** The record has a particular object. Jews "could never be targeted at a high enough level to constitute a real threat without bringing down the entire juridical order and converting it into a global order of hostage taking." The blockchain therefore records the edge where judgment threatens to give way to the hunt: "Measurements of this ever present 'penumbra' of another possibility against the terms of juridical order is what is to be measured on the civilizational blockchain" ([p-19](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-19)). His example is the genocide charge against Israel. The demand that the accusation mirror the worst crimes committed against Jews is "precisely the kind of thing to record" ([p-15](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-15)).

## How it follows from the originary hypothesis

The essay never names the hypothesis. The connection runs through several of Katz's intermediate concepts, which can be taken as a chain.

**Deferral leaves a sign that must be defended.** On the originary scene, a gesture holds off the collective rush on the central object. Katz stresses that "any act of deferral leaves behind it a sign, which can be repeated by someone other than myself, and provides a starting point for the next act of deferral: to defend that sign" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-6)). A ledger that can't be altered is a way of defending signs of deferral: promises, judgments, title deeds. In a recent essay he makes the link directly: "A promise is meant to lock you in and now we have blockchains for that" ([Promise, Fraud…](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-11)).

**The center distributes, and that distribution is the nomos.** Once the center is occupied by a Big Man, a king, or an empire, the shared meal of the originary scene becomes an originary allotment of land and authority. Katz reads the founding covenant in exactly these terms. It is a covenant "with the creator of the universe, which is to say the founder of the original nomos" ([p-12](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-12)). Following Bernard Lamborelle, he reads it as originally a land grant from a Mesopotamian king, later raised into a covenant with God. That reading "unites service to earthly governance with commitment to eternity and always mediated through the juridical, the space of judgment" ([p-13](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-13)). The Hebrew Bible then becomes "the longest, most convoluted, revised and thickly imagined title deed possible," whose layers keep evidence of an unbroken chain of transmission ([title deed essay](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack#p-11)).

**Writing is ledgering of debt to the center.** "The first writing is the first designation of property and the first token of exchange and issuance of debt" ([Tokenization](/post/tokenization#p-1)). This is why "Jews are better thought of as a nation of scribes than a nation of priests" ([p-13](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-13)), or, in the earlier essay, "a nation of priests became a nation of scribes which means a nation of ledgerers" ([A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-6)).

**The juridical is the institution of deferral.** Katz defines the juridical as "placing a ceiling on the vendetta by introducing higher order arbitration… while, on the other end, preserving what is ultimately a ritually enacted originary nomos" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-1)). Hostility to Jews reverses this. It is a vendetta that must break through the ceiling. A people whose vocation is keeping the ledger of judgment is therefore the direct counterpart of the scapegoating movement aimed at it.

**Scapegoating is accusation against the center.** Katz writes that "antisemitism" is "really about giving a name to hidden sources of power, which in the West always involves some kind of 'prosecution' of 'tyrants'" ([The Political Infrastructure of Judaism](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-3)). The Jews became that name because they sit "in the imperative gap (between the issuance and enactment of the imperative)" ([p-13](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-13)). They are the intermediaries between empires and their subjects, "(self) created as a people serving imperial interests" ([Cybernetics](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-3)). The blockchain vocation turns that exposed position into a public role, played openly. As he puts it elsewhere, "It's better to be obnoxious than appear to be hiding" ([Cybernetics](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-23)).

**This is not martyrdom.** Katz observes that the Jewish people played "a role analogous to Jesus… but without offering themselves up as a willing sacrifice" ([Political Infrastructure](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-24)). The blockchain proposal is consistent with his general effort to keep the Axial Age insight into the innocent victim while dropping the victimary politics built on it. Witnessing is done by recording and exercising power, not by suffering. He states plainly that "Being a civilizational blockchain, though, involves exercising power" ([p-15](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-15)).

Two cautions. Katz says the Lamborelle reading is his own and "Other Jews need not accept this account" ([p-13](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-13)). His theology is also stripped down: "God's voice is whatever tells us when and how to defer violence, or when and how we are failing to do so" ([Cybernetics](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-9)). That is the originary hypothesis showing through, and observant readers may find it too thin.

## What to read next

- [A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism) gives the earlier version: persecutions read as lessons about failures of mediation, and a proposal to make "contributes to good governance" a criterion in halakhic reasoning.
- [The Longest, Most Convoluted… Title Deed](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack) is the full reading of scripture as a chain-of-custody document, which supplies the "ledger" with its contents.

A question to take further: Katz says the blockchain should record treatment of Jews "on the scale of justice." Take a current dispute, a campus case or a contested property claim in Jerusalem, and ask what would be entered on the ledger. Which part belongs to the juridical, and which part is the "penumbra" of hostage-taking that he wants measured?
